Suppose first that $\mathcal{T}$ is irreducible.  Then the results in \cite{CPZ08} show that any nonnegative eigenvector is positive, and that this eigenvector
is unique up to a scalar factor. 
 It corresponds to a positive eigenvalue which is the spectral radius of $\mathcal{T}$.  Furthermore, the characterization in \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} holds.


 Assume that $\mathcal{T}\geqslant 0$ is not irreducible.  First, we shall use

a perturbation argument to deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ is a eigenvalue of $\mathcal{T}$ corresponding
 to a nonnegative eigenvector satisfying \eqref{noneigwkir}.  Let $\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be a tensor all the entries of which are $1$.  Assume that $\epsilon>0$.  Then $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d}>0$.  Hence there exists a positive probability vector $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)$ so that
 \[(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})(\mathbf{u}(\epsilon))=\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d})\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)^{\circ(d-1)}.\]
 From the first characterization \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} we deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ is a nondecreasing function on $(0,\infty)$.
 Since $\rho(\mathcal{S})$ is a continuous function in $\mathcal{S}\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{sp}$ it follows that $\lim_{\epsilon\searrow 0}\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$.
 Observe next that there exists a decreasing sequence $\epsilon_j>0, j\in\mathbb{N}$ converging to zero such that $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)$ converge to a probability vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$.    Since $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)=(u_{1,j},\ldots,u_{n,j})^\top$ is an eigenvector of $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d}$ corresponding to $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ we deduce \eqref{noneigwkir}.
 
 The results in \cite[\S3]{nuss86} yield that for any nonnegative tensor $\mathcal{T}$ with maximal nonnegative eigenvalue $\rho(\mathcal{T})$, the characterization \eqref{infmaxcharrho}
 holds.  (To apply the results in \cite{nuss86} we need to consider the homogeneous map of degree one $\mathbf{u}\mapsto (\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u}))^{\circ\frac{1}{d-1}}$ for $\mathbf{u}\geqslant \0$.
 Here for $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^\top\geqslant \0$ we denote by $\mathbf{u}^{\circ t}$ the vector $(u_1^t,\ldots,u_n^t)^\top$ for $t>0$.  See for more details \cite{FGH}.)
 One can also use the above perturbation technique to deduce 

\eqref{infmaxcharrho}.

The statements of the theorem for a weakly irreducible tensor $\mathcal{T}$ follow
from~\cite[Corollary 4.2]{FGH}.

Consider the convex function $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}'):=\sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)$ on the hyperplane $H=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\sum_{i=1} x_i=0\}$.
 Observe that since the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{T}$ are positive we obtain that each expression $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i e^{-(d-1)x_i}\geqslant t_{i,\ldots,i}$.  That is $ u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)\geqslant u_iw_i \log t_{i,\ldots,i}$ for each $i\in [n]$.
 We claim, as in \cite{FK75}, that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$ for any sequence $\mathbf{x}_k=(x_{1,k},\ldots,x_{n,k})^\top\in H$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty} \|\mathbf{x}_{k}\|=\infty$. 
 Indeed by taking a subsequence and renaming the coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ we can assume the following conditions.  First $x_{1,k}\leqslant \ldots\leqslant x_{n,k}$ for each positive integer $k$.  Furthermore, there there exists $l\in [n-1]$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_{i,k}=-\infty$ for $i\in[l]$, and $x_{l+1,k}\geqslant a (\in\mathbb{R})$  for each positive integer $k$. Since $\mathcal{T}'$ is irreducible there $i\in[l-1]$ and $j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\in[n]\setminus [l-1]$ such that $t_{i,j_1,\ldots,,j_{d-1}}>0$.  Hence
$\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}\geqslant t_{i,j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}}e^{(d-1)(a-x_{i,k})}$.  Thus
$\lim_{k\to \infty}\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}=\infty$, which implies that  $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$.  Hence $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ achieves its minimum at some critical point $\mathbf{y}\in H$. Let $\1=(1,\ldots,1)^\top$.  Observe that $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')=f(\mathbf{x}+t\1)$ for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
Thus the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is achieved at each point of the form $\mathbf{y}+t\1$.
We now study the effects of rescaling of $\mathcal{T}'$.  First, consider the rescaling $\tilde\mathcal{T}=[\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Second,  consider the rescaling $\hat\mathcal{T}=[\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{\sum_{j=2}^d b_{i_j}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$.  Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat\mathcal{T})$ is achieved at the points $\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{b}+t\1$.  Now choose $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{y}-\log\mathbf{u}$.  Then the minimum  of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat\mathcal{T})$ is achieved at the point $\log\mathbf{u}$.  Finally, rescale $\hat\mathcal{T}$ to obtain $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for a unique $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$.   In particular $\rho(\mathcal{T})=1$ and \eqref{pratTuid} holds.  Therefore the first equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds.  As $\log\mathbf{u}$ is a minimal point of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T})$ we deduce by  straightforward calculations that the second equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds.

\label{ocmstocmat}  Denote by $\operatorname{Stoc}(n)\subset \mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ the convex set of (row) stochastic matrices.  Then there exists  a map  $\Psi_n: \Omega(n)\to \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ and a multivalued map
$\Phi_n: \operatorname{Stoc}(n)\to\Omega(n)$
with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For each $A\in \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ the set $\Phi_n(A)$ is a closed nonempty 

convex set of occupation measures. 
\item $\Phi_n(A)$ consists of a unique occupation measure if and only if $1$ is a simple root of $\det(zI-A)$.
\item If $A\in \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ is irreducible then $\Phi_n(A)$ consists of a unique occupation measure $\mu(A)$ which is irreducible.  Furthermore, $\Psi_n(\mu(A))=A$. 
\item If $\mu\in\Omega(n)$ is irreducible then
$\Psi_n(\mu)$ is irreducible  and  $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))=\{\mu\}$.
\item For each $\mu\in\Omega(n)$ the convex set $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))$ contains $\mu$.


 \end{enumerate}

Assume that $A\in \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$.  Let $\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)^\top$ be the stationary distribution corresponding to $A$.  So $\mathbf{z}$ is a probability vector satisfying $A^\top\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}$.  A straightforward computation shows that $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{z})A\in\Omega(n)$.
We define $\Phi_n(A)$ to be the set of all occupation measures of this form. 

   Hence $\Phi_n(A)$ is a closed convex set.  This proves part \emph{1}.
Furthermore $\Phi_n(A)$ consists of one occupation measure $\mu(A)$ if and only if $\mathbf{z}$ is unique, i.e., $1$ is a geometrically  simple eigenvalue.  
It is a classical property of stochastic matrices that the geometric and algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$ coincide, see Theorem 6.5.3 in \cite{Fribook}; hence, $1$, is an algebraically simple eigenvalue. 

This proves part \emph{2}.
Clearly, if $A$ is irreducible then $\mathbf{z}>\0$ is unique and $\mu(A)$ is irreducible.

We now define $\Psi_n(\mu)$.  Suppose first that $\mu$ does not have a zero row.  Let $r_i=\sum_{j=1}^n \mu_{ij}$.  Then $\Psi_n(\mu):=\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(r_1^{-1},\ldots,r_n^{-1})\mu$.  Note that $\mathbf{z}=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)^\top$ is a probability vector satisfying
$\Psi_n(\mu)^\top \mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}$.  Hence $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))$ contains $\mu$.  Clearly, if $\mu$ is irreducible then $\Psi_n(\mu)$ is irreducible.  Parts \emph{3} and \emph{4} follow straightforwardly. 

Assume now that $\mu$ has zero rows.  Let $S(\mu)\subset [n]$ be the subset of all zero rows of $\mu$.  As $\mu$ is an occupation measure, $S(\mu)$ is also the subset of zero columns of $\mu$.  Let $k$ be the cardinality of $S(\mu)$.  Then $\mu$ is a direct sum of $\mu_1\oplus 0_{k\times k}$, where $\mu_1\in\Omega(n-k)$ with nonzero rows, and
$0_{k\times k}$ is the $k\times k$ zero matrix.  Let $J_k\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$ be the matrix whose all entries are $1$.  Then $\Psi_n(\mu)=\Psi_{n-k}(\mu_1)\oplus \frac{1}{k}J_k$.
Clearly, $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))$ contains $\mu$ in this case.  This completes the proof of part \emph{5}.

Assume first that $A>0$.  The for each $\mu>0$ we have inequality \eqref{auxlemAG1}.  Hence
\begin{eqnarray*}
\log\rho(A)\geqslant\sup_{\mu=[\mu_{i,j}]\in\Omega(n), \mu>0} \sum_{i,j\in[n]} \mu_{ij}\log \frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}=\\ \sup_{\mu=[\mu_{i,j}]\in\Omega(n)} \sum_{i,j\in[n]} \mu_{ij}\log \frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
Choose $\mu$ as in \eqref{maxmu} to deduce \eqref{AGchar1}.

Assume now that $A\geqslant 0$ but not positive. 
First observe that if $a_{ij}=0$ and $\mu_{ij}>0$ then 
$\mu_{ij}\log\frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n\mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}=-\infty$.  Hence $\sum_{i,j=1}^n 
\mu_{ij}\log\frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n\mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}=-\infty$. 
Suppose that $\rho(A)=0$.  Then $\log\rho(A)=-\infty$.  Since a support of $A$ does not contain a dicycle we deduce that $\sum_{i,j=1}^n 
\mu_{ij}\log\frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n\mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}=-\infty$ for each $\mu\in\Omega(n)$.  Therefore \eqref{AGchar1} holds in this case.

Suppose that $A=[a_{ij}]$ is irreducible.  So $\log\rho(A)>-\infty$.  The above arguments imply that it is enough to show
\begin{equation}\label{AGchar2}
\log\rho(A)=\max_{\mu=[\mu_{i,j}]\in\Omega(n,\supp{A})} \sum_{i,j\in[n]} \mu_{ij}\log \frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}.
\end{equation}
For $\mu\in\Omega(n,\supp{A})$ such that $\supp{A}=\supp{\mu}$ we can use Lemma \ref{auxlemAG} to deduce \eqref{AGchar2} as for $A>0$.  

It is left to show for \eqref{AGchar1}  for a nonnilpotent nonirreducible $A$.
Let $J_n\in\mathbb{R}^{ns n}_+$, where each entry of $J_n$ is $1$.  Consider $A(\varepsilon)=A+\varepsilon J_n$, where $\varepsilon>0$.  Then $\rho(A)<\rho(A(\varepsilon)$.  As $\log a_{ij}<\log(a_{ij}+\varepsilon)$, and the theorem holds for $A(\varepsilon)$, it follows that
\[\log\rho(A(\varepsilon)) >\sup_{\mu=[\mu_{i,j}]\in\Omega(n)} \sum_{i,j\in[n]} \mu_{ij}\log \frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}.\]
Letting $\varepsilon\searrow 0$ we deduce the inequality 
\[\log\rho(A)\geqslant\sup_{\mu=[\mu_{i,j}]\in\Omega(n)} \sum_{i,j\in[n]} \mu_{ij}\log \frac{a_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^n \mu_{ik}}{\mu_{ij}}.\] 
Assume that $A_1$ is an irreducible principle submatrix of $A$ such that $\rho(A)=\rho(A_1)$.  Then $\supp (A_1)\subset S\times S$ for some minimal nonempty subset of $[n]$.  Consider $\Omega(n,S\times S)$.  Now apply the theorem for the irreducible $A_1$ to deduce the theorem in this case.

The proof of this theorem is analogous to the proof of Theorem \ref{AGchar} and we repeat briefly the analogous arguments.  Fix a weakly irreducible tensor $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$.  Assume that $\mu=[\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \Omega(n^{\times(d-1)})$ has the same support as $\mathcal{T}$.  Let $\nu=[\nu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be the following weakly irreducible tensor
\[\nu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=\frac{\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}{x_{i_1}}, \;x_{i_1}={\sum_{j_2,\ldots,j_d\in[n]}\mu_{i_1,j_2,\ldots,j_d}}, \quad i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n].\]
Let $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^\top $  Since $\mu$ is a weakly irreducible tensor and an occupation measure if follows that $\mathbf{x}$ is a positive probability vector. 
Clearly $\nu\otimes^{d-1}\1_n=\1_n$.  Hence $\rho(\nu)=1$ and the corresponding eigenvector is $\1_n$.  Recall that $D\nu(\mathbf{x})=(d-1) \nu\times \otimes^{d-2} \mathbf{x}$ (\eqref{partderT}).  Hence, the entries for the matrix $A(\mu)=(d-1)D\nu(\1_n)=[a_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$, defined in \eqref{defATu} , are given by
\[a_{ij}=\frac{d-1}{x_i}\sum_{i_3,\cdots,i_d\in[n]}\mu_{i,j,i_3,\cdots,i_d}, \quad i,j\in[n].\]
Since $\mu$ is an occupation measure it follows that $\mathbf{x}^\top A(\mu)=\mathbf{x}^\top$
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i a_{ij}=(d-1)\sum_{i,i_3,\cdots,i_d\in[n]}\mu_{i,j,i_3,\cdots,i_d}=x_j \;\forall j\in[n].\]

Fix a tensor $\mathcal{B}=[b_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps}^{n^{\times d}}$ such that $b_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$ if $\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$.  Let $\mathcal{C}(t)=[\nu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}e^{tb_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be the log-convex function on $\mathbb{R}$.  Clearly, each $\mathcal{C}(t)$ is weakly irreducible. 
Hence $\log\rho(\mathcal{C}(t))$ is a convex differentiable function on $\mathbb{R}$.  As in the proof of Lemma \ref{auxlemAG}, the variational formula \eqref{rhoTpert} implies that 
\[\log(\rho(\mathcal{C}(t))'(t=0)= \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} \mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}b_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}.\]
The convexity of $\log\rho(\mathcal{C}(t)$ and the equality $\log\rho(\mathcal{C}(0))=\log\rho(\nu)=0$ yield that inequality 
\[\log\rho(\mathcal{C}(1))\geqslant \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} \mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}b_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}.\]
Choose 
\[b_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=\log\frac{t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}{\nu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}} \textrm{ if } t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}>0.\] 
Note that $\mathcal{C}(1)=\mathcal{T}$.  Hence 
\begin{equation}\label{baslogrineqten}
\log\rho(\mathcal{T})\geqslant \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n]}\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\log\frac{t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\sum_{j_2,\ldots,j_d\in[n]} \mu_{i_1,j_2,\ldots,j_d}}{\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}.
\end{equation}
The density argument yields that the above inequality holds for any $\mu\in\Omega(n^{\times(d-1)},\supp \mathcal{T})$.  Let $\mu\in\Omega(n^{\times(d-1)})$ and assume that $\supp \mu$ is not contained in $\supp \mathcal{T}$.   Hence there exists a positive entry of $\mu$:  $\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ such that $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$.   Therefore 
\[\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\log\frac{t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\sum_{j_2,\ldots,j_d\in[n]} \mu_{i_1,j_2,\ldots,j_d}}{\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}}=-\infty.\]
In this case \eqref{baslogrineqten} trivially holds.  These arguments show that $\log\rho(\mathcal{T})$ is not less that the right-hand side of \eqref{entropcharsrten1}.

As $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{u}=1$ it follows that $\mu$ is a probability tensor.  Let $A(\mathcal{T})$ be defined as in \eqref{defATu}. The equality \eqref{logeqtenT} is deduced in a similar way the equality in Lemma \ref{auxlemAG}.  

 Assume now that $\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is not weakly irreducible.  As in the proof of Theorem \ref{AGchar} it follows that the inequality \eqref{baslogrineqten} holds.  Suppose first that $\rho(\mathcal{T})=0$.  Then $\log\rho(\mathcal{T})=-\infty$.  Hence \eqref{entropcharsrten1} trivially holds.  Equivalently, for each $\mu\in\Omega(n^{\times (d-1)})$ there exists $i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n]$ such that $\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}>0$ and $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$.
 
 Assume now that $\rho(\mathcal{T})>0$.    Let $\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be a symmetric tensor whose all entries are $1$. Our arguments yield that there exists positive occupation measure $\mu(l)=[\mu_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}(l)]\in\Omega(n^{\times (d-1)})$ such that 
 \[\log\rho(\mathcal{T}_l)=\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_d\in [n]}
\mu_{i_1,\dots, i_d}(l) \log \Big(\frac{(\sum_{k_2,\dots, k_d}\mu_{i_1,k_2,\dots, k_d}(l))(t_{i_1,\dots, i_d}+\frac{1}{l})}{\mu_{i_1,\dots, i_d}(l)}\Big) \enspace .\]
As $\Omega(n^{\times (d-1)})$ is a compact set, there is a subsequence of $\{\mu(l)\},l\in \mathbb{N}$ which converges to the occupation measure $\mu\in\Omega(n^{\times (d-1)})$.  Hence
\[\log\rho(\mathcal{T})=\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_d\in [n]}
\mu_{i_1,\dots, i_d} \log \Big(\frac{(\sum_{k_2,\dots, k_d}\mu_{i_1,k_2,\dots, k_d})t_{i_1,\dots, i_d}}{\mu_{i_1,\dots, i_d}}\Big) \enspace .\]
Combine this equality with  the inequality \eqref{baslogrineqten} to deduce the theorem in this case.

The ergodic control interpretation of the logarithm of the spectral radius, explained in \Cref{subsec-ergodic}, extends to the case of nonnegative tensors.
The set of actions of the player is still the finite set $[n]$. 
The set of actions in state $i$ consists of probability
measures $p=(p_{i,i_2,\dots,i_n})_{i_2,\dots,i_n}$ on the set $S_i:= \{(i_2,\dots,i_d)\in [n]^d\mid a_{i,i_2,\dots,i_n}>0$. If an action $p$ is selected, the next
state becomes $j$ with probability $\sum_{2\leqslant k\leqslant n,\;\; i_k = j} p_{i,i_2,\dots,i_n}$. Then, the player receives the payment 
\[
\operatorname{KL}_i(p,\mathcal{T})= -\sum_{(j_2,\dots,j_d)\in S_i} p_{i,i_2,\dots,i_d}\log(p_{i,i_2,\dots,i_d}/t_{i,i_2,\dots,i_d}) \enspace.
\]
We leave it to the reader to check, arguing as in \Cref{subsec-ergodic}, that 
the value of the associated ergodic game is independent of the initial
state as soon as $\mathcal{T}$ is weakly irreducible, and that Formula~\eqref{logeqtenT}
allows us to identify $\log \rho(\mathcal{T})$ to the value of this game.

We say that a nonzero nonnegative vector $u$ is a \emph{tropical eigenvector}
of the tensor $\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$, with the associated \emph{tropical eigenvalue} $\lambda$ if


\[
\max\{t_{i,i_2,\ldots,i_d}u_{i_2}\ldots u_{i_d},\;i_2,\ldots,i_d\in[n]\} = 
\lambda u_i^{d-1} \enspace,\qquad i\in [n] .
\]
The existence of a tropical eigenvector $u$ follows from a standard
application of Brouwer's theorem.

Formula~\eqref{tropspecradchar} follows from the Collatz-Wielandt characterization of the spectral radius of a non-linear map~\cite{nuss86}. The existence

from the generalized Perron-Frobenius theorem~\cite[Theorem 2]{GG04}. 
When $\mathcal{T}$ is irreducible, it is straightforward to check that any
nonnegative eigenvector must be positive.

Let $V'\subset [n]$ will be the smallest subset of indices for which the coordinate $v_i$ of the tropical eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ satisfying \eqref{tropspeceig} with the following restriction. For each $i\in V'$ $v_i>0$ and the corresponding maximum in \eqref{tropspeceig} can be taken only on $i_2,\ldots,i_d\in V'$.


For each $k\in V'$,
we choose indices
$i_2=j_2(k),\ldots,i_d=j_d(k)\in V'$
achieving the maximum in \eqref{tropspeceig}, so that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-saturate}
t_{i,j_2(i),\ldots,j_d(i)} v_{j_2(i)}\ldots v_{j_d(i)}
 = \rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{T}) v_i^{d-1}, \qquad i\in V'.
\end{equation}




This defines a digraph $\gamma$.  The minimality of $V'$ implies that $\gamma\in\Sigma_{n,d-1}$ is a $(d-1)$-dicycle.  Let $\mathbf{u}(\gamma)$ be defined from $\gamma$,
as in~\eqref{defleAgam}.
We now raise each term of the $i$th equality~\eqref{eq-saturate} to the power
$u(\gamma)_i$, 
\begin{equation}\label{e-saturate2}
(t_{i,j_2(i),\ldots,j_d(i)} v_{j_2(i)}\ldots v_{j_d(i)} )^{u(\gamma)_i}
 = (\rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{T})v_i^{d-1})^{u(\gamma)_i}, \qquad i \in V' \enspace .
\end{equation}
We next multiply all the equalities~\eqref{e-saturate2}, and observe
that, thanks to~\eqref{defleAgam}, the terms involving powers of $v$ can be canceled, showing that




\[ \rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{F})= w(\gamma,\mathcal{F})
\leqslant \max_{\gamma'\in\Sigma_{n,d-1}} w(\gamma',\mathcal{F})
\enspace.\]
We show the reverse inequality. Given $\gamma\in \Sigma_{n,d-1}$ let $\mathcal{F}(\gamma)=[f(\gamma)_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$ be the following symmetric tensor in the last $d-1$
 indices: $f(\gamma)_{i,i_2,\ldots,i_d}=f_{i,i_2,\ldots,i_d}$ if an only if $i\in V(\gamma)$ and  $(i_2,\ldots,i_d)$ are permutations of $(j_2(i,\gamma),
 \ldots,j_d(i,\gamma)$.  Otherwise $f_{i,i_2,\ldots,i_d}=0$.  Clearly, $\mathcal{F}(\gamma)\leqslant \mathcal{F}$.  Hence $\rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{F}(\gamma))\leqslant \rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{F})$.
 Arguing as in the first part of the proof, we show that $\rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{F}(\gamma))=w(\gamma,\mathcal{F})$.  Hence we have characterization \eqref{chartropeigten1}.

\log t_{i_1,\dots,i_d} + u_{i_1} + \dots +u_{i_d} &\leqslant \lambda + (d-1) u_{i_1} ,

\label{e-ineqlp}
\end{eqnarray}
In particular, $\log\rho_{\mathrm{trop}}(\mathcal{T})$ can be computed in polynomial time
in the Turing model of computation, assuming that the input consists
of the set $\bar{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{T})$ and 
of numbers $\log t_{i_1,\dots,i_d} \in \mathbb{Q}$ for $(i_1,\dots,i_d)\in

nodes.statement: It follows from the above linear programming formulations that logrho_trop coincides with the value of an ergodic Markov decision process (MDP), i.e., a one player stochastic game with mean payoff, in which the state space is [n]. This game appears to be ``a degeneration'' of the game with entropic payment in Remark~, in which now, the action spaces become finite. Let us describe this MDP. In a given state j, the set of actions consists of \(j,i_2,dots,i_d)in barS(T)\, the player receives the payment log t_j,i_2,dots ,i_d, the next state become k with probability |\2leqslant ellleqslant dmid i_ell =k\|/(d-1), and log rho_trop represents the best mean payoff per time unit. Then, the digraphs gamma arising in the combinatorial characterization~ correspond to feedback policies, and this characterization shows that log rho_trop is the supremum of the ergodic payments attached to the different feedback policies, a general property of ergodic Markov decision processes. The dual variables mu_i_1,dots,i_d represent an occupation measure, giving the frequency at which an action (i_1,dots,i_d) is played.

It follows from the above linear programming formulations
that $\log\rho_{\mathrm{trop}}$ coincides
with the value of an ergodic Markov decision process (MDP), i.e.,
a one player stochastic game with mean payoff~\cite{whittle86},
in which the state space is $[n]$. This game appears
to be ``a degeneration'' of the game with entropic 
payment in Remark~\ref{rem-ergodiccontrol}, in which now, the action spaces
become finite.  

Let us describe
this MDP. In a given state $j$, the set
of actions consists of $\{(j,i_2,\dots,i_d)\in \bar{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{T})\}$,
the player receives the payment $\log t_{j,i_2,\dots ,i_d}$, 
the next state become $k$ with probability $|\{2\leqslant \ell\leqslant d\mid 
i_\ell =k\}|/(d-1)$, and
$\log \rho_{\mathrm{trop}}$ represents the best mean payoff per time unit.
Then, the digraphs $\gamma$ arising in the combinatorial
characterization~\eqref{chartropeigten1} correspond to feedback policies,
and this characterization shows that $\log \rho_{\mathrm{trop}}$ is the
supremum of the ergodic payments attached to the different
feedback policies, a general property of ergodic Markov decision processes~\cite[Prop.~7.2]{AG03}.
The dual variables $\mu_{i_1,\dots,i_d}$ represent
an {\em occupation measure}, giving the frequency
at which an action $(i_1,\dots,i_d)$ is played.

We suppose here, without loss of generality, that the tensor is symmetric in the last 3 indices. We next list the different cycles appearing in the representation of Crefchartropeigten. First, there are two 3-cycles with vertex set of cardinality 1 (multiloops). The first of these 3-cycles arises by considering the multigraph gamma^1_1, with vertex set V_1^1=\1\ and edges multiset E^1_1=\(1,1), (1,1),(1,1)\, meaning that edge (1,1) is repeated 3 times. Then, the adjacency matrix A(gamma^1_1) is the 1times 1 matrix equal to (3), the associated invariant measure u(gamma^1_1) is the one-dimensional vector (1), leading to the weight w(gamma^1_1) =t_1111 enspace . Similarly, there is another 3-cycle gamma^1_2 with vertex set of cardinality 1, namely V^1_2=\2\, with edge multiset E^1_2=\(2,2),(2,2),(2,2)\, leading to the weight w(gamma^1_2) =t_2222 enspace . Less trivial examples arise when considering 3-cycles with vertex set of cardinality 2, like gamma_1^2, with vertex set V^2_1=\1,2\ and edge multiset E^2_1=\(1,1),(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,1),(2,1)\. The associated adjacency matrix is \[ A(gamma_1^2)= left(cc 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 right) \] with invariant measure u(gamma^2_1)= (3/4,1/4), leading to the weight w(gamma_1^2)= t_1112^3/4t_2111^1/4 enspace . This suggests the following rule to construct all the 3-cycles with a vertex set of cardinality 2: -- in state 1, select one of the terms at the right hand side of~ except the first term t_1111v_1^3 (which would lead to a multiloop), --- in state 2, select one of the terms at the right hand side of~, except the first term t_2222v_2^3; Then, the exponents of the terms which are selected determine the edges of the multigraph. Take $n=2$ and $d=4$. Then, the general tropical eigenproblem
  can be written as follows, 
\begin{eqnarray}
  \lambda v_1^3 & =& \max(t_{1111}v_1^3,\,
   t_{1112}v_1^2v_2, \, t_{1122}v_1v_2^2,\,
  t_{1222}v_2^3)\label{e-eq-t1}
\\
\lambda v_2^3 &=&
\max(t_{2111}v_1^3,\,
  t_{2112}v_1^2v_2, \, t_{2122}v_1v_2^2,\,
  t_{2222}v_2^3)
\enspace .\label{e-eq-t2}
\end{eqnarray}
We suppose here, without loss of generality, that the tensor
is symmetric in the last $3$ indices.





We next list the different cycles appearing in the representation
of \Cref{chartropeigten}.

First, there are two $3$-cycles with vertex set of cardinality $1$ (multiloops).
The first of these $3-$cycles arises by considering the multigraph $\gamma^1_1$, with vertex set $V_1^1=\{1\}$ and edges multiset $E^1_1=\{(1,1), (1,1),(1,1)\}$, meaning that edge $(1,1)$ is repeated $3$ times.
Then, the adjacency matrix $A(\gamma^1_1)$ is the $1\times 1$ matrix equal to $(3)$, the associated invariant measure $u(\gamma^1_1)$ is the one-dimensional vector $(1)$, leading to the weight


  \begin{equation}
       w(\gamma^1_1)  =t_{1111} \enspace .\label{e-gamma1}
  \end{equation}
  Similarly, there is another $3$-cycle $\gamma^1_2$ with vertex
  set of cardinality $1$, namely $V^1_2=\{2\}$,
  with edge multiset $E^1_2=\{(2,2),(2,2),(2,2)\}$,
  leading to the weight
    \begin{equation}
       w(\gamma^1_2)  =t_{2222} \enspace .\label{e-gamma2new}
    \end{equation}
    Less trivial examples arise when considering $3$-cycles
    with vertex set of cardinality $2$, like $\gamma_1^2$,
    with vertex set $V^2_1=\{1,2\}$ and edge multiset
    $E^2_1=\{(1,1),(1,1), (1,2),
  (2,1)$, $(2,1),(2,1)\}$. The associated adjacency matrix is
  \[
  A(\gamma_1^2)= \left(\begin{array}{cc} 2 & 1 \\
    3 & 0 \end{array}\right)
  \]
  with invariant measure $u(\gamma^2_1)= (3/4,1/4)$,
  leading to the weight
  \begin{equation}
    w(\gamma_1^2)= t_{1112}^{3/4}t_{2111}^{1/4} \enspace .\label{e-gamma2}
  \end{equation}
  This suggests the following rule to construct all the $3$-cycles
  with a vertex set of cardinality $2$: 
  --  in state $1$, select one of the
  terms at the right hand side of~\eqref{e-eq-t1}
  except the first term $t_{1111}v_1^3$ (which would lead to a multiloop),
  --- in state $2$, select one of the
  terms at the right hand side of~\eqref{e-eq-t2},
  except the first term $t_{2222}v_2^3$;
  Then, the exponents of the terms which are selected
  determine the edges of the multigraph.
  For instance, selecting
  $t_{1112}v_1^2v_2$ in state $1$, and
  $t_{2111}v_1^3$ in state $2$, yields
  the exponent vectors $(2,1)$ and $(3,0)$,
  corresponding precisely to the rows of the
  matrix $A(\gamma_1^2)$. It follows
  that there are precisely $9$ $3$-cycles not reduced
  to multiloops, corresponding
  to these different selections. We next
  list the adjacency matrices of all these
  $3$-cycles, and the associated weights,
  \begin{eqnarray*}
    \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c}
      
            \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        2 & 1 \\
         3 & 0      \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
      \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        2 & 1 \\
         2 & 1      \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
            \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        2 & 1 \\
         1 & 2            \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                        \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        1 & 2 \\
        3 & 0                        \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                        \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        1 & 2 \\
         2 & 1                        \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                        \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        1 & 2 \\
         1 & 2                        \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                                                \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        0 & 3 \\
        3 & 0                        \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                        \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        0 & 3 \\
         2 & 1                        \end{smallmatrix}\right) &
                        \left(\begin{smallmatrix}
        0 & 3 \\
        1 & 2                        \end{smallmatrix}\right)\\ &&&&&&&\\ 
                        \scriptstyle t_{1112}^{3/4}t_{2111}^{1/4}& \scriptstyle t_{1112}^{2/3}t_{2112}^{1/3}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1112}^{1/2}t_{2122}^{1/2}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1122}^{3/5}t_{2111}^{2/5}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1122}^{1/2}t_{2112}^{1/2}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1122}^{1/3}t_{2122}^{2/3}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1222}^{1/2}t_{2111}^{1/2}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1222}^{2/5}t_{2112}^{3/5}&
                        \scriptstyle t_{1222}^{1/4}t_{2122}^{3/4}








      \end{array}
    \end{eqnarray*}
  \Cref{chartropeigten} shows that the tropical spectral
  radius of $\mathcal{T}$ is given by the maximum of the weights~\eqref{e-gamma1},
  \eqref{e-gamma2new} and of the weights appearing in the latter table.

nodes.statement: Corollary~ leads to a polynomial time algorithm to compute the spectral radius of a tropical tensor. The reduction to ergodic Markov decision processes allows us, more generally, to apply any algorithm developed in this setting, including policy iteration. For huge scale instances, iterative power type algorithms may be more suitable. One may use the relative value iteration. This algorithm does converge if the optimal strategies satisfy a certain cyclicity condition (Corollary~5.9 and Theorem 6.6 of ). One can also use the projective Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration described in, section 5, which is a power type algorithm with damping that converges without any condition of cyclicity.
